topics.summary: An orchestrator records workflow state and decides which command to issue next. Choreography lets participants react to events without one central step controller. Both can work, but each distributes reasoning differently.

topics.title: 21.2.1 Persisting Commands, Results, and Timers
topics.summary: A workflow engine must survive losing its process memory. Persist the current state, the identity of issued commands, relevant results, and the information needed to resume waiting or retrying. A sleeping thread is not a durable timer.

cards.question: Explain Persisting Commands, Results, and Timers in your own words.
cards.answer: A workflow engine must survive losing its process memory. Persist the current state, the identity of issued commands, relevant results, and the information needed to resume waiting or retrying. A sleeping thread is not a durable timer.

blocks.text: When a step command and state transition must remain consistent, use a local transaction and outbox pattern. Record that the step is pending and record the outgoing command together. On restart, reissue the same command identity under the downstream idempotency contract.

topics.title: 21.2.2 Deduplicating Events Without Erasing Conflicts
topics.summary: The model maps event identity to event kind. Repeating the same identity and kind is a duplicate and causes no new transition. Reusing the same identity for another kind is a conflict. This prevents a replay from changing its meaning silently.

cards.question: Explain Deduplicating Events Without Erasing Conflicts in your own words.
cards.answer: The model maps event identity to event kind. Repeating the same identity and kind is a duplicate and causes no new transition. Reusing the same identity for another kind is a conflict. This prevents a replay from changing its meaning silently.

topics.title: 21.3.1 Understanding Why Compensation Is Not Time Travel
topics.summary: Compensation is another business action that aims to restore an acceptable condition. It may not reverse every consequence of the original action. A refund can incur fees, a released reservation may no longer be available, and a sent notification cannot be unsent from a recipient’s memory.

topics.title: 21.3.2 Reconciling Stuck and Ambiguous Workflows
topics.summary: A reconciliation process compares durable workflow state with authoritative downstream state. It can detect a step whose response was lost, a compensation that remains pending, or an externally completed action not yet reflected locally. Reconciliation is part of the design, not evidence that the normal path was useless.

It can detect a step whose response was lost, a compensation that remains pending, or an externally completed action not yet reflected locally. Reconciliation is part of the design, not evidence that the normal path was useless.

Manual repair must preserve identity and auditability. Provide commands such as retry step, confirm external receipt, or request compensation with recorded reason and actor. Directly flipping a status column can bypass invariants and leave pending outbox commands that later run unexpectedly.

Define an escalation age for stuck workflows and a responsible owner. A dashboard containing thousands of permanently “in progress” rows is not operational control. Include the last successful transition, last attempt, current authority, and next eligible action in diagnostic state.

For the lab service, a pending job has a simpler recovery path: replay the same worker command until a result can be recorded, subject to its documented limitations. Extending it to a saga requires additional durable states and commands rather than just adding more network calls inside the dispatcher loop.

reading.title: Engineering case — Handle cancellation while a charge outcome is unknown
paragraphs: A workflow reserves capacity and sends a charge command. The charge response is lost. The user requests cancellation. The workflow cannot safely assume either that no charge occurred or that a charge definitely occurred. Its state must represent uncertainty and preserve the original charge identity.

A reconciliation step can query the payment authority using that identity, or repeat the same idempotent charge request if the provider’s contract makes that safe. If the charge is confirmed, the workflow can issue a separately identified refund or other compensation. If it is confirmed absent and no in-flight action can still create it under the protocol, the workflow can release the reservation without claiming a refund happened.

A late charge success can arrive after cancellation begins. The orchestrator should associate it with the original step and update the recovery obligation, not discard it because the current UI says cancelled. A user-visible cancellation request and completed compensation are different states.

The compensation itself can have an uncertain reply. It needs its own stable identity and status path. Reusing the original charge key for a semantically different refund can violate the provider’s identity contract; generating a new refund identity on every retry can duplicate compensation. Operation type and logical intent must remain explicit.

The local saga model uses a simplified compensated event to acknowledge completion. It does not perform or verify a real refund. A production implementation should refine that event’s meaning according to the external authority and preserve the corresponding receipt or reference.

An operator repair command should not merely overwrite state to cancelled. It should record the evidence used, the actor, the intended reconciliation transition, and any remaining external obligation. Otherwise the normal dispatcher may later issue a command that the manual edit forgot to remove or supersede.

This scenario explains why a saga is not a distributed rollback instruction. It is a stateful recovery process that must account for partial knowledge, repeated messages, and actions whose consequences cannot be erased instantaneously.
